extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Kantian philosophy / aesthetics (scholars, advanced undergraduates)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Kant’s criteria and norms for making and assessing judgements of taste, beauty, and the sublime; aimed at guiding analysis of aesthetic judgment and art/poetry/speech within a Kantian framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty of judging of the beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis of judgements of taste must show what is required to call an object beautiful; Kant analyses the 'moments' of such judgements (he treats the moment of quality first because aesthetical judgement first pays attention to it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of Aesthetic Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement upon an object of satisfaction may be quite disinterested, i.e. not based upon an interest; judgements of taste do not in themselves establish any interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disinterestedness means absence of desire to possess the object (Mendelssohn noted: contemplation with quiet satisfaction even though not in our possession). Only in society does having taste become 'interesting' (social interest), but pure aesthetic judgements remain disinterested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity Requirement for Aesthetic Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement must be 'pure', i.e. not mingled either with concepts of the Object or with sensations as determining grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a judgement is mixed with concepts or sensations, its claim to the special privilege (e.g., universal assent) is an inaccurate application. Purity is necessary if the judgement's reference is merely to the formal condition of the cognitive powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for Claiming Universal Assent of an Aesthetic Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be justified in claiming universal assent for an aesthetical judgement it is sufficient to assume (1) subjective conditions of the judgement, as regards relation of the cognitive powers thus put into activity to a cognition in general, are the same in all men; and (2) the judgement refers merely to this relation (to the formal condition) and is pure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition (1) is grounded on the communicability of representations/knowledge among humans; condition (2) excludes contamination by concepts or sensations. A failure on (2) only shows inaccurate application, not the invalidity of the privilege in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure: Practical vs Contemplative (Taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical pleasure is that necessarily bound up with desire of an object (may be cause or effect of desire); contemplative (passive) satisfaction is pleasure not bound up with desire, and the feeling of the latter kind is called 'taste'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction locates taste as a contemplative, passive satisfaction rather than a desire-driven pleasure; clarifies what kind of affect underlies aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as Purposiveness Without Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: An object (e.g., a flower) is regarded as beautiful because in perceiving it we find a certain purposiveness which, in our judgement, is referred to no purpose at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with objects that indicate purposiveness for a definite use (e.g., manufactured implements): if we regard something as a work of art with a definite purpose, we typically do not have immediate pure satisfaction. Beauty involves perceived purposiveness not judged as serving a particular end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of Taste for Arts of Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Models of taste as regards the arts of speech must be composed in a dead and learned language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two reasons given: (1) dead languages avoid the inevitable change and fashioning of living languages (noble expressions become flat, new creations short-lived); (2) learned languages have grammar not subject to wanton change and rules are preserved unchanged. This is practical advice for exemplars/models used to teach taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction Between Aesthetic and Teleological Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: In the aesthetical judgement we view beautiful nature with favour and have a free (disinterested) satisfaction in its form; in a teleological judgement we pay attention to the reference of natural forms to purposes and may regard such purposiveness as 'a favour of nature' ministering to our culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes two modes of assessing natural form: pure form-satisfaction (aesthetic) vs consideration of functional/purposeful ordering (teleological). They yield different kinds of judgements and reasons for approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature and Regularity as Aesthetic Indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfectly regular countenance ordinarily tells us nothing because it contains nothing characteristic; the exaggeration of a characteristic such that it does violence to the normal Idea (the purposiveness of the race) is called 'caricature'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularity may indicate mediocrity; genius is marked by departure from ordinary proportions. Caricature is an aesthetic anti-pattern: exaggerated traits violate the ideal purposiveness and do not produce the same aesthetic satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affections vs Passions: Criterion for Sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Affections are related merely to feeling and are stormy and unpremeditated; passions belong to the faculty of desire and are steady inclinations that render determination of the will by principles difficult or impossible. Passions abolish freedom and therefore cannot be called sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublimity involves a relation to freedom (affective states that do not abolish freedom can be sublime), while passions (which abolish freedom) cannot be legitimately termed sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric vs Beautiful Art (Speech Evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readiness and accuracy in speaking (together constituting Rhetoric) belong to beautiful art; but the art of the orator (ars oratoria) that avails itself of the weaknesses of men to move them like machines is worthy of no respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of spoken art should separate technical aesthetic qualities (style, accuracy) from manipulative rhetorical aims; a 'vir bonus discendi peritus' (the orator without art but of great impressiveness) who unites imagination and sympathy with the good is an ideal, though not always realized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trichotomy Necessity for a priori Synthetic Division
rubrics_metrics.description: If an a priori division is to be synthetical (derived from a priori concepts), the division must be threefold (trichotomy): there must be (1) a condition, (2) a conditioned, and (3) the concept arising from their union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a methodological criterion for structuring a priori philosophical analyses and divisions (e.g., of faculties or moments) and explains why Kant's divisions in pure philosophy are commonly threefold.
